title: TB8-00920
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): XXXX XXXX (the "Appellant") is a citizen of Turkey and is appealing a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) denying his claim for refugee protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX (the "Appellant") is a citizen of Turkey and is appealing a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) denying his claim for refugee protection. The Appellant argues that the RPD erred in its assessment of the objective basis for his risk upon return to Turkey. After careful review of the evidence in the record, the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) finds that the RPD failed to consider key documentation regarding similarly-situated persons and failed to consider the Appellant's forward-looking risk on the basis that he would be perceived to be a supporter of the XXXX movement if he returned to Turkey.
For the reasons provided below, I allow the appeal and find the Appellant is a Convention refugee.

The Appellant alleges that he joined the Turkish Armed Forces in XXXX 2012 and that he was a XXXX XXXX at the Turkish Military Academy. After the attempted coup in Turkey on July 15, 2016, he alleges that the government started targeting and purging cadets from the military due to their perceived involvement in the attempted coup, for which he states he was not involved. The Appellant claims that many military people were arrested and tortured following the coup, including many of his fellow cadets. As a result of this purge, he and other cadets were transferred to other universities. Upon graduation, his university diploma noted that it was provided by XXXX University under the auspices of XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, which he alleges effectively blacklists him as a member of XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX and for having been involved in the attempted coup. In XXXX 2017, he obtained a student visa and arrived in Canada in February 2017. The Appellant made an inland claim for refugee protection in May 2017. If he returns to Turkey, he fears detention, arrest, torture, and/or being subject to an unfair trial due to the perception that he is a member of XXXX. Further details are provided in his Basis of Claim (BOC) Form, and his testimony at the RPD hearing.1 The RPD's Decision

The Appellant had a refugee determination hearing on July 26, 2017. In a written decision issued on November 16, 2017, the RPD rejected the claim. The RPD panel found the Appellant did not have an objective basis for his fear of persecution, as there is a chance of persecution, not a reasonable chance of persecution. Therefore, the RPD concluded that the Appellant does not have a well-founded fear of persecution on a Convention ground, or that he would not personally be subjected to a risk to life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or a danger of torture upon return to Turkey.

For questions of fact, mixed fact and law, and law, the RAD applies the standard of correctness in accordance with the Federal Court of Appeal's decision in Huruglica.2 In assessing findings involving the credibility of oral testimony, the RAD may apply the modified standard of reasonableness in situations where the RPD enjoys a meaningful advantage.3 Unless otherwise stated in the reasons, the RAD uses the correctness standard on all findings and will consider the overall refugee determination on a standard of correctness, even where the RAD has deferred on some or all findings. ADMISSIBILITY OF EVIDENCE SUBMITTED ON APPEAL

Evidence from the person who is the subject of the appeal is only admissible on appeal if it meets one of the statutory conditions set out in subsection 110(4) of the IRPA, namely that it arose after, or was not reasonably available, or the person could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented the evidence at the time the claim was rejected. If one of these conditions is met, the RAD will then consider if the evidence is credible, relevant, and new as endorsed by the Federal Court of Appeal in Singh.4

The Appellant does not clearly list the documents he is submitting as new evidence. However, based on my review of the Appellant's Record, the Appellant appears to submit four documents as new evidence, all of which postdate the RPD's decision rejecting his claim. 1) Memurlar.net, "XXXX operation in 49 cities: 240 people were taken into custody", dated 30 November 2017;5 2) Memurlar.net, "16 of 20 suspects, who were taken into custody, were sent to prison", dated 25 December 2017;6 3) Memurlar.net, "Operation against XXXX Private Military Structure", dated 17 January 2018;7 and, 4) National Documentation Package (NDP) for Turkey, dated 21 December 2017.8

The Appellant does not provide fulsome submissions in compliance with rule 3(3)(iii)(g) about how these documents meet the requirements of 110(4). That said, I accept the first three documents listed above as new evidence. They postdate the RPD's decision and describe events in Turkey since the Appellant's claim was rejected. As a result, the documents and its contents could not have been provided at the time of the rejection of his claim. In addition, the documents are "relevant" to describing the treatment of persons similarly-situated to the Appellant. They are also "credible" as I have no reason to doubt the source and circumstances in which this information was reported and came about. For these reasons, I find the Singh criteria are met in this case and I admit the articles from Memurlar.net as new evidence.

With respect to the updated NDP package, I observe that the Appellant's own memorandum chooses to rely on the content of the NDP dated March 31, 2017, which was the version of the NDP before the RPD. The Appellant does not indicate what information in the updated NDP is new or relevant to the issues in this appeal. I have reviewed the updated NDP and find that in the absence of submissions from counsel about how the updated NDP is relevant, or what it adds to the documentary evidence already in the record, I find the relevance and newness factor in Singh is not established. Furthermore, in my review of the updated NDP, nothing turns on the updated content, nor does it impact the disposition in this appeal.

Finally, I note that the Appellant provided two recent RAD decisions in his Appeal Record, which were decided since the Appellant's RPD decision.9 However, I will not consider this as new evidence, as this is appropriately considered case law relied upon in the Appellant's submissions. Case law is not evidence. Should the RAD convene an oral hearing?

The Appellant does not specifically request an oral hearing based on this new evidence. Although I have found documentary evidence admissible as new evidence, I find that the new evidence does not raise a serious issue with respect to the credibility of the person who is the subject of the appeal. Therefore, the criteria of 110(6) is not met and an oral hearing is not necessary in this case.10 DETERMINATIVE ISSUE

The determinative issue is whether the RPD erred in its analysis of the Appellant's objective risk on the basis of his perceived involvement in XXXX or as a supporter of the XXXX movement.11 ANALYSIS Well-founded Fear of Persecution The Appellant's Argument

The Appellant argues that the underlying facts of his allegations were not disputed by the RPD and should be considered as credible. In addition, the Appellant argues that the RPD significantly and erroneously downplayed the objective documentary evidence about the risk to him if he returned to Turkey by finding there was a "chance", but not a "reasonable chance" of persecution if he returned to Turkey as a dismissed XXXX XXXX. He submits that it is obvious from the record that XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX and the closure of the military schools was the government's response to its belief that XXXX had infiltrated the schools and that they were targeting military cadets. This is supported by President Erdogan's statement that he believes that 95% of the military cadets are "XXXX". Despite this, the RPD seems to conclude that the Appellant somehow falls into the 5% of cadets who are not perceived as being affiliated to XXXX. There is also no dispute that cadets in Turkey are arrested and detained at accelerating rates, and as such, there is no basis for the RPD's conclusion that the evidence demonstrates the opposite. The evidence shows that the Appellant was dismissed from the military as a result of the closure of the military schools, an action taken by the Turkish government in response to its belief that XXXX had infiltrated these schools and the cadets were accordingly affiliated with XXXX. He also notes that many of his family members including his aunt and cousin have been reported to the authorities on the suspicion of being members of the XXXX Movement.

With respect to the RPD's finding that he was able to exit Turkey, the Appellant argues that this finding is contrary to the case law, which states this is not determinative and that the assessment must be forward-looking. He submits he is not required to show that he is wanted by the authorities. On a forward-looking assessment, the Appellant states that the documentary evidence shows that military cadets continue to be arrested and detained for their perceived XXXX involvement. In this respect, the Appellant argues that the RPD ignored evidence submitted in the record of similarly-situated individuals and additional news articles about the treatment of former military cadets in Turkey. This included a positive RPD decision of the Appellant's friend, which is based on the same facts as a former XXXX XXXX. The RAD's Assessment

I agree with the Appellant's argument and find the RPD erred. The RPD ignored key evidence in the documentary evidence, including of similarly-situated individuals. In addition, I agree with the Appellant that the RPD did not dispute the underlying facts of the case, which were that the Appellant was a XXXX XXXX and dismissed following the attempted coup. It also did not dispute that his diploma indicated that it was awarded under the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, which was implemented shortly after the attempted coup. Based on my review of the record, I find the Appellant credible in these core allegations, and therefore, the determinative issue is whether the Appellant's profile as a dismissed XXXX XXXX places him at a forward-looking risk of persecution. For the reasons that follow, I find that his claim is well-founded.

Amnesty International reports that "[a]nyone with any perceived link to the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX accused of orchestrating the coup, has been targeted. Soldiers, police, judges, lawyers, academics, journalists, teachers, doctors and even football referees. Seemingly, no one is immune."12 Item 4.11 of the NDP says that the Turkish government has called XXXX (XXXX XXXX XXXX) a terrorist organization. The document goes on to say that Human Rights Watch notes that being labelled a terrorist group allows Turkey to apply "overbroad terrorism laws against suspected XXXX." This document expressly states that the Turkish government's "purge" has gone too far beyond its scope and is now targeting people based on their perceived association with XXXX. Those who have been detained have been "subjected to beatings and torture, including rape, in official and unofficial detention centres in the country." Trials of those arrested and charged have been criticized as not preserving defendants' rights to a fair trial, due process and legal remedies.13

The rhetoric towards XXXX supporters and sympathizers also indicates a clear intention of state authorities to "cleanse" Turkey of all of its elements,14 demonstrating an overall context of fear and risk of harm to those seen as XXXX supporters. President Erdogan has called XXXX supporters "viruses" and called on Turkish citizens to report them to prosecutors and security agencies, even if they are your friends.15 The Turkish President has called on Turks to inform on their fellow citizens, and so the whispered word of a neighbour with a grudge could be enough to land someone in jail.16 This initiative is not limited to within Turkey's borders, as the European Commission reports that members of the Turkish diaspora are under pressure to report to Turkish authorities XXXX sympathizers they know who reside in their communities abroad, and that Erdogan threatens that no region in the world is a safe haven for XXXX sympathizers.17 The NDP states that the government is a taking a maximalist position in purges, by going after those who have simply an affinity with or membership of the XXXX network, rather than going after those who actually participated in the coup.18

The Council of Europe (CE) states that the government's emergency decree-laws had an extremely wide scope of application, the use of vague terms such as "contacts", "relations" or "connections" and the way they were being implemented. The report also noted the serious administrative sanctions with a permanent character, such as dismissals, arrests and detention measures that seem to be decided upon weak or in some cases seemingly non-existent evidence and vague criteria, such that simple denunciation might lead to someone being sent to prison. There is also an undisclosed list of 16 criteria used by authorities to identify those suspected of having connections, relations and contacts with "XXXX".19

The documentary evidence indicates that XXXX XXXX XXXX introduced on XXXX XXXX, 2016, made major changes to the army, announcing the discharge of military staff and the shutdown of all military schools, academies and non-commissioned officer training institutes. The decree also stated that students who continued their studies in war schools, faculty and colleges will be registered to appropriate faculties and colleges.20 On August 3, 2016 it was reported that at least 4,000 students were affected by the decree to close all military high schools and military academies and that the schools were closed because the government believes that they have been infiltrated by XXXX and that about 95% of the student body identifies with XXXX.21 The Appellant is one such person affected.

The documentary evidence in the record from the Appellant shows that the Turkish state has arrested and detained soldiers and cadets, and that there is a continuing interest of the Turkish state in persons similarly-situated to the Appellant. This includes cadets being arrested, detained and placed on probation,22 and evidence that the government dismissed 22,920 military personnel despite the fact that only 8,651 personnel, including cadets and conscripts, took part in the coup attempt.23 In addition to the Appellant's own credible testimony about fellow cadets he knows who have been dismissed, detained and arrested due to their perceived involvement in the attempted coup, the Appellant submitted documentation as new evidence illustrating that the government is not done arresting and detaining military personnel, including cadets.24

In this case, the Appellant has provided his armed forces card and his diploma from XXXX University that refers to XXXX XXXX XXXX, which would identify him as a person of concern to Turkish authorities for having attended a military academy that was closed. Military academies that the President has stated 95% of the cadets were XXXX supporters. The Appellant stated that he has sought redress by bringing a case against the Turkish government, but to date there has been no outcome. Given the concerns about the arbitrariness of the judicial process and lack of access to justice in Turkey following the attempted coup, it is plausible that the Appellant will be unable to clear his name. As a result, his university degree designated under XXXX XXXX has effectively blacklisted him as a perceived XXXX and member of XXXX.

The documentary evidence provided by the Appellant illustrates the lack of redress, as well as the ostracization and socio-economic cost to persons and family members who have been blacklisted for perceived support or affiliation with the XXXX XXXX.25 In this regard, I note that the Appellant provided evidence that his cousin, a military officer, was accused of being affiliated with the XXXX XXXX and was detained and tortured. His aunt was also dismissed from her job, detained and then released on probation. I have no reason to doubt the Appellant's credibility on this fact. In this respect, and in light of the documentary evidence above, the constant fear of arrest for supporting the XXXX XXXX, the widespread dismissals, cancelled passports, difficulty obtaining new employment, the freezing of assets and the financial insecurity, the atmosphere of suspicion and the stigma attached to being a XXXX in today's Turkey, and the continuing arbitrariness to arrest and detention for actual or perceived involvement in the XXXX XXXX, even to those who have not participated in the attempted coup, amounts to a sustained violation of basic human rights and to a well-founded fear of persecution.

Given the Appellant's undisputed identity as a XXXX XXXX, who was dismissed and transferred to another university, as well as his diploma being designated as such under XXXX XXXX, the evidence indicates that he is likely to be perceived as affiliated with the "XXXX", also known as the XXXX or XXXX XXXX. As such, I find the Appellant possesses a profile that is subject to more than a mere possibility of persecution by the Turkish state on a forward-looking basis. The Appellant has a nexus to the Convention, being either perceived "political opinion" or perceived "membership in a particular social group". Furthermore, I find that there is no state protection or internal flight alternative for him as the state is the agent of harm and exists everywhere in the country. Finally, in regard to the RPD's finding about the Appellant's ability to exit Turkey without being of interest to authorities, I find this is not determinative. The test is forward-looking and it is possible the authorities had not yet turned their mind to him. Therefore, I find the Appellant is a Convention refugee.

Pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(b) of the IRPA, the RAD sets aside the determination of the RPD and substitutes its determination that the Appellant is a Convention refugee, as he has a well-founded fear of persecution on the basis of his perceived membership in a particular social group, and/or imputed political opinion as a member of XXXX or as a supporter of the XXXX XXXX XXXX This appeal is allowed.
